item.title: Anger is Healthy if You Can Understand and Deal with It
item.description:
Anger

Anger is Healthy if You Can Understand and Deal with It

These strategies can help you feel more in control of your anger.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • Anger is a normal and can spur you into positive action, however it can also lead to unhealthy aggression.
  • Assuming others have negative intent can fuel your anger.
  • Intentionally trying to see others as complex human beings can help soothe your anger.

There is a powerful quote attributed to Buddha, "Holding onto anger is like drinking poison and expecting the other person to die."

This article provides you with an opportunity to start reflecting on how anger shows up in your life and how you can practice some coping strategies to help you channel your anger into healthy action.

Source: Simran Sood / Unsplash

Recognize what fuels anger.

Many things in your daily life can make you to feel angry, from minor inconveniences to major injustices around the world. According to the American Psychological Association, anger is an emotion characterized by tension in response to perceived injustice (e.g., feeling devalued), frustration, and/or real or imagined injury.

Anger can spur you into action to right a wrong. For example, people continually speed down your street when there are children playing outside. Your anger at that situation may lead you to rally your neighbors, gather signatures, and advocate for speed bumps to be placed on your street during a local township meeting.

Unfortunately, anger can take a toll on your own health.1,2 Anger can also get you into trouble if it leads to aggression (i.e., behavior that is intended to inflict harm or damage, whether physical or mental, on another person or object). You can feel angry without acting aggressively. Your anger could instead lead to positive behavior, such as reflection, self-soothing, and taking healthy action. One way to soothe your anger is to check in on the story you are telling yourself in the moment.

What story are you telling yourself?

Part of what can lead you to act aggressively is the story you tell yourself or the assumptions of negative intent you make in a situation. For example, say someone cuts in front of you in the checkout line at the store. The story you tell yourself has a significant impact on how you feel.

If you tell yourself that the person intentionally wanted to cut in front of you to make you feel bad, then you likely will feel angry and may act aggressively (for example, by yelling at them). Conversely, if you tell yourself that the person didn't see you, you may still feel angry but likely less so. You might offer them the kindness you hope others would extend to you if you made the same error.

A helpful strategy is to notice and challenge the assumptions you are making about other people's intent when you start to feel angry. It's important to notice when you are assuming negative intent.

Challenge yourself to come up with at least three alternative explanations. For a person who seemingly cuts in line, you might consider if they have a hearing or sight impairment, or whether they just got off the phone with a family member who was yelling at them to hurry home, if they might desperately need to use the bathroom, or if they need to rush to pick their children up from school.

See others as complex beings.

It can be helpful to give others the same consideration you hope you would be given in a similar situation. You would likely hope that others could see you as a complex and layered human being who sometimes makes mistakes.

Say you are at a restaurant and see someone yelling at the server. You might automatically feel angry because you see a potential injustice taking place. You are likely making a lot of automatic assumptions about the person who is yelling.

article continues after advertisement

Consider asking yourself the following questions:

  • What has led them to act this way?
  • What needs are they trying to get met right now?

These questions can help you identify alternative explanations. Maybe the person started yelling because there is someone with a disability at their table and they asked the server calmly for a reasonable accommodation four separate times and now, on the fifth time, they have lost their patience and started to yell. And while it may not excuse their behavior, considering this alternative might allow you to cool your anger and have more empathy for them in that moment.

Say you were at the same table with the person who is yelling, you might take an additional step in considering how you can calmly express that you understand their needs and would also like them to approach the situation in a healthier way in the future.

Overall, it's important to remember to be kind to yourself as you work to manage your anger, because the reality is you will never be perfect at controlling your anger. No one is. But you can make ongoing efforts that can help you feel more in control of your anger.

You can find additional strategies in my new pocket-sized book, How to Understand and Deal with Anger.
